idiom_name: AutoCloseable + try-with-resources (close() as the release contract)
implementation_notes: Java absorbs the pattern into the language: implement java.lang.AutoCloseable (or java.io.Closeable when close may only throw IOException) and declare the resource in a try-with-resources header so close() runs on every exit path, in the reverse order of creation, with an exception from the body taking precedence and the close exception attached as suppressed. AutoCloseable.close is explicitly not required to be idempotent - unlike Closeable.close - so an owner that may be closed twice must guard itself (AtomicBoolean/state flag), and the javadoc advises relinquishing the resource and marking it closed before throwing. Cascade is the owner's job: close() releases owned resources and never borrowed ones. Finalizers are deprecated in current Java, so they are not a fallback strategy.
pitfalls: AutoCloseable.close is allowed to be non-idempotent; the compiler calls it once, but any manual call or a duplicated resource variable can close twice - guard the implementation.
Resources are closed before the catch/finally blocks of the same try statement run, so compensating code sees an already-closed resource.
A lambda or object escaping the try-with-resources block can capture the closed resource; the compiler only warns for effectively-final resource variables used outside the block.

variants.name: java.lang.ref.Cleaner as the backstop for native resources
variants.idiom_name: Cleaner.register + a static cleaning-state Runnable (replaces finalize())
variants.implementation_notes: For a resource that also wraps native memory or a handle, the deterministic path stays try-with-resources, but the safety net should be java.lang.ref.Cleaner instead of a finalizer: register the object with a Runnable cleaning action that holds no reference to it, and the action runs at most once after the object becomes phantom reachable - unless the explicit close() already invoked it through the returned Cleanable. The javadoc shows exactly the shape used here: a static state class capturing the resource, a Cleaner.Cleanable field, and close() delegating to clean(). Exceptions thrown by cleaning actions are ignored and cleaner behaviour during System.exit is unspecified, which is why this is a net and never the release contract.
pitfalls: The cleaning action must not capture the outer instance (use a static nested class, not an inner/lambda form), or the object never becomes phantom reachable and the action never runs.
Cleaner actions run on a cleaner thread at an unspecified time and their exceptions are ignored: assert the explicit close() path in tests, never the cleaning action.
Double-free: the explicit close() and the cleaning action must share one state object so the native address is cleared exactly once.
